``` ::: ::: # Drawing Bar Plots ## Basic Bar Plots with Seaborn ### Basic Bar Plot ::: {#d58d7bc5 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Basic bar plot: the x-axis is categorical, and the y-axis shows the mean by default. # The black error bars show 95% confidence intervals. sns.barplot(data=df, x='island', y='body_mass_g') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=602 height=429} ::: ::: ::: {#643062bb .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # estimator='sum': use the sum as the bar height instead of the default mean sns.barplot(data=df, x='island', y='body_mass_g', estimator='sum') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=619 height=429} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.barplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.barplot.html)** (`estimator` parameter) ::: {#8e6e1486 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.__version__ # View the current Seaborn version. Since 0.13, the default is a single color to avoid meaningless color distinctions. ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` '0.13.2' ``` ::: ::: ::: {#e0024799 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Check: the mean body mass for Biscoe Island is the bar height shown in the chart. df.loc[df['island'] == 'Biscoe', 'body_mass_g'].mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 4716.017964071856 ``` ::: ::: ### Count Plot ::: {#296213e1 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Count plot: automatically counts the number of observations in each category sns.countplot(data=df, x='species') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=593 height=429} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.countplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.countplot.html)** ## Grouping Bars and Removing Error Bars Use the `hue` parameter to group by category, and set `errorbar=None` to remove error bars. ::: {#dfa0d9e0 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Group by sex with hue, and remove error bars with errorbar=None sns.barplot(data=df, x='island', y='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=602 height=429} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.barplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.barplot.html)** (`errorbar` and `hue` parameters) ## Rotating Tick Labels When x-axis labels are too long, use `plt.xticks()` to rotate them: ::: {#10221b7e .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.barplot(data=df, x='island', y='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') # Rotate labels by 45 degrees. ha='right' aligns the right edge of each label with the tick. plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=602 height=472} ::: ::: **Reference: [`plt.xticks()` documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.xticks.html)** (`kwargs` section) [Wilke (2019, chap. 6.1)](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-amounts.html#bar-plots) suggests that when labels are dense, a horizontal layout is easier to read than rotated labels: ::: {#77455b66 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Swap the x and y axes: a horizontal layout is easier to read when labels are dense. sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-1.png){width=633 height=429} ::: ::: The same idea applies to count plots: ::: {#9d66df48 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.countplot(data=df, y='species', hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-21-output-1.png){width=632 height=429} ::: ::: ## Setting the Global Theme ::: {#fbae7581 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Set the global plotting theme. It applies to all subsequent Seaborn charts. # Use sns.reset_orig() to restore the default theme. sns.set_theme(font_scale=1.2, style='darkgrid') ``` ::: `sns.set_theme()` sets the global plotting theme for all later Seaborn charts. Call `sns.reset_orig()` to restore the default theme. ::: {#9c124f9f .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Define a chart object named ax ax = sns.barplot( data=df, x='body_mass_g', y='island', errorbar=None, hue='sex', ) # Set the title and axis labels ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-23-output-1.png){width=653 height=462} ::: ::: After assigning a Seaborn chart to the variable `ax`, you can call Matplotlib methods on it for further customization, similar to assigning a DataFrame to `df` and then calling its methods. **Note the difference between these two:** - `sns.set()` / `sns.set_theme()`: Seaborn **global** theme-setting functions. They are equivalent, but `sns.set_theme()` is preferred. - `ax.set()`: a Matplotlib method for a **specific chart object**, used to set titles, axis labels, and related elements. **References:**\ [`sns.set()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.set.html)\ [`sns.set_theme()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.set_theme.html#seaborn.set_theme)\ [`ax.set()` documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.set.html) ## Adjusting the Legend Whether you use `errorbar=None` or `errorbar=('ci', 0)`, the legend may cover the plot, so you may need to adjust its position manually with `sns.move_legend()`. ::: {#eee8d704 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} # errorbar=None: the legend is automatically placed on the right ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-24-output-1.png){width=653 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#015fe56d .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # errorbar=('ci', 0): the legend is automatically moved away from the error-bar area ax = sns.barplot( data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=('ci', 0), hue='sex', ) ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-25-output-1.png){width=653 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#33c282f1 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') # Combine bbox_to_anchor with loc: move the legend's loc reference point to (0.5, -0.2) sns.move_legend(ax, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.2), loc='upper center', ncols=2) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-26-output-1.png){width=653 height=549} ::: ::: ::: {#07ad512b .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') sns.move_legend(ax, loc='lower right') # Set loc only: move the legend to the lower right of the plot plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-27-output-1.png){width=653 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#70a85047 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') # Place the upper-left corner of the legend at (1, 1) relative to the axes sns.move_legend(ax, loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1)) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-28-output-1.png){width=784 height=462} ::: ::: **References:**\ [`sns.move_legend()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.move_legend.html) (`obj` and `loc` parameters)\ [`matplotlib.axes.Axes.legend()` documentation](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.axes.Axes.legend.html) (`loc`, `ncols`, and `bbox_to_anchor` parameters) ## Changing Colors Use the `palette` parameter to change chart colors. It can take the following kinds of values: 1. **Seaborn predefined palette names** (default: `'deep'`): `'deep'`, `'muted'`, `'bright'`, `'pastel'`, `'dark'`, `'colorblind'` 2. **Matplotlib colormap names**: for example, `'viridis'`, `'plasma'`, `'coolwarm'`, `'Blues'`, `'Reds'` 3. **HLS/HUSL color models**: `'hls'`, `'husl'` 4. **Cubehelix schemes**: `'ch:'`, for example `'ch:s=0.5,r=-0.5'` (colorblind-friendly and suitable for grayscale printing) 5. **Gradients**: `'light:'`, `'dark:'` 6. **Blends**: `'blend:,'` 7. **Lists of color codes**: hexadecimal codes such as `['#FF5733', '#33FF57']`, RGB tuples, or Matplotlib color names ::: {#291f834d .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Default palette ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') sns.move_legend(ax, bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), loc='upper left') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-29-output-1.png){width=784 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#184bfc00 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} # palette='flare': use a predefined Seaborn palette ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex', palette='flare') ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') sns.move_legend(ax, bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), loc='upper left') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-30-output-1.png){width=784 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#b99698d5 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Pass a list of Matplotlib color names to palette ax = sns.barplot(data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex', palette=['blue', 'orange']) ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') sns.move_legend(ax, bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), loc='upper left') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-31-output-1.png){width=784 height=462} ::: ::: ::: {#3c5c97e9 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Pass a list of hexadecimal color codes to palette ax = sns.barplot( data=df, y='island', x='body_mass_g', errorbar=None, hue='sex', palette=['#a1c9f4', '#8de5a1'], ) ax.set(title='Penguin', xlabel='Body Mass (g)', ylabel='Island') sns.move_legend(ax, bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), loc='upper left') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-32-output-1.png){width=784 height=462} ::: ::: **References:**\ [Seaborn `sns.set_theme()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.set_theme.html) (`palette` parameter)\ [Seaborn `sns.color_palette()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.color_palette.html) (list of predefined palette names)\ [Matplotlib named colors](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/color/named_colors.html)\ [Matplotlib colormaps](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/colors/colormaps.html)\ [w3schools color picker](https://www.w3schools.com/colors/colors_picker.asp) ## Extension: Counting Penguins on Each Island {.unnumbered} The following two approaches are equivalent and can be used later to sort bar plots by totals. **Method 1: `df.groupby().size()`** ::: {#fa11588f .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Group by island and count the number of rows in each group df.groupby('island').size() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` island Biscoe 168 Dream 124 Torgersen 52 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: **Method 2: `df.value_counts()`** ::: {#935f17bc .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Count the occurrences of each value in the island column df.value_counts('island') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` island Biscoe 168 Dream 124 Torgersen 52 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: # Drawing Other Plots ## Point Plot The y-axis of a bar plot must start at 0 to ensure that the visual proportions match the data proportions, following Wilke's [Principle of Proportional Ink](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/proportional-ink.html) ([Wilke 2019, chap. 17](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/proportional-ink.html)). Point plots do not have this restriction: the y-axis can start from the data range, and the data-ink ratio is higher because there is less visual clutter. When the x-axis is nominal data, such as island names, the points do not need to be connected with lines. ::: {#8f2fe1cb .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} # linestyle='none': do not connect points when the x-axis is categorical. # The vertical segments around points are error bars. sns.pointplot(data=df, x='island', y='body_mass_g', hue='sex', linestyle='none') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-35-output-1.png){width=614 height=440} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.pointplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.pointplot.html#)** ## Histogram The x-axis of a bar plot represents **discrete categories** (nominal or ordinal data). The x-axis of a histogram represents **continuous numerical intervals** (ratio data). ::: {#f20bda52 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-36-output-1.png){width=595 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#939cc433 .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Group with hue: plot penguins from each island separately and overlay the distributions sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', hue='island') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-37-output-1.png){width=595 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#595f6ce8 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Use a consistent y-axis range to compare the plot with and without hue grouping sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm') plt.show() sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', hue='island') plt.ylim(0, 80) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-38-output-1.png){width=595 height=440} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-38-output-2.png){width=595 height=447} ::: ::: ::: {#966b2965 .cell execution_count=38} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.histplot( data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', hue='island', stat='density', # The total area of all bins is 1 (probability density) common_norm=False # Normalize each group separately. If True, all groups share one total area of 1. ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-39-output-1.png){width=609 height=440} ::: ::: ### The `stat` Parameter This parameter controls the statistic shown by the histogram. Available values include: - `'count'`: bin height = number of data points in the bin. - `'frequency'`: bin height = count / bin width, or frequency per unit width. This is useful when bin widths are unequal. - `'probability'` / `'proportion'`: bin height = count / total count, so all bin heights sum to 1. - `'percent'`: bin height = (count / total count) * 100, so all bin heights sum to 100. - `'density'`: bin height = frequency / bin width, so the total **area** of all bins is 1. As bin width approaches 0, this becomes a smooth density curve. ::: {#454a0d6e .cell execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code} # stat='count': bar height = number of data points in each bin ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', stat='count') # Iterate over each bar (patch), get its height, and show a value label above it for p in ax.patches: # Get the bar height, which is the frequency in the interval height = p.get_height() # Add text ax.text( p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, # x coordinate: center of the bar height, # y coordinate: bar height int(height), # text: integer frequency ha='center', va='bottom', # horizontal/vertical alignment ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-40-output-1.png){width=595 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#fb7ac73e .cell execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code} # stat='frequency': bar height = count / bin width ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', stat='frequency') for p in ax.patches: height = p.get_height() ax.text( p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, height, int(height), ha='center', va='bottom', ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-41-output-1.png){width=595 height=445} ::: ::: ::: {#94e60c7c .cell execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} # stat='probability': bar height = count / total count, and all bar heights sum to 1 ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', stat='probability') for p in ax.patches: height = p.get_height() ax.text( p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, height, f'{height:.2f}', # Keep two decimal places ha='center', va='bottom', ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-42-output-1.png){width=609 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#8ad8df2b .cell execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} # stat='percent': bar height = (count / total count) * 100, and all bar heights sum to 100 ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', stat='percent') for p in ax.patches: height = p.get_height() ax.text( p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, height, int(height), ha='center', va='bottom', ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-43-output-1.png){width=595 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#c37300bb .cell execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} # stat='density': bar height = frequency / bin width, and the total bin area is 1 ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', stat='density') for p in ax.patches: height = p.get_height() ax.text( p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2, height, f'{height:.3f}', ha='center', va='bottom', ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-44-output-1.png){width=619 height=440} ::: ::: ### The `common_norm` Parameter This boolean parameter only applies when `stat` is `'probability'`, `'proportion'`, `'percent'`, or `'density'`. Its default value is `True`: - `common_norm=True`: normalize using the **entire dataset**, so bin heights can be compared across groups. - `common_norm=False`: normalize each **subgroup independently**, so bin heights are only meaningful within each group. ::: {#c9b0d200 .cell execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.histplot( data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', hue='island', stat='density', common_norm=True, # Overall normalization: the total bin area across all groups is 1 ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-45-output-1.png){width=629 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#4738dd09 .cell execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.histplot( data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', hue='island', stat='density', common_norm=False, # Separate normalization: each group's bin area sums to 1 ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-46-output-1.png){width=609 height=440} ::: ::: When overlapping groups are difficult to read, use `data=df[df['column']==value]` to filter the data and plot each group separately: ::: {#64da4c9e .cell execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Plot by island to avoid overlapping groups and inspect each island's distribution separately ax = sns.histplot( data=df[df['island'] == 'Torgersen'], x='flipper_length_mm', stat='density' ) ax.set(title='Torgersen Island', xlabel='Flipper Length (mm)') plt.show() ax = sns.histplot( data=df[df['island'] == 'Biscoe'], x='flipper_length_mm', stat='density' ) ax.set(title='Biscoe Island', xlabel='Flipper Length (mm)') plt.show() ax = sns.histplot( data=df[df['island'] == 'Dream'], x='flipper_length_mm', stat='density' ) ax.set(title='Dream Island', xlabel='Flipper Length (mm)') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-47-output-1.png){width=609 height=462} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-47-output-2.png){width=619 height=462} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-47-output-3.png){width=609 height=462} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.histplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.histplot.html)** (`hue`, `stat`, and `common_norm` parameters) ## Box Plot A box plot summarizes a distribution with five key values: min, Q1, Q2 (median), Q3, and max. It also marks outliers beyond the whisker range. - **Box**: from Q1 to Q3, containing the middle 50% of the data. - **Line inside the box**: the median (Q2). - **Whiskers**: extend outward from Q1 and Q3, by default to the extreme values within 1.5 * IQR. - **Outliers**: points beyond the whisker range, marked separately. ![Normal distribution and IQR](../../../src/img/ttl/amt-dist/normal-dist.png) **Box Plot vs. Histogram** ![Box plot](../../../src/img/ttl/amt-dist/boxplot.png) Box plots are useful for quickly identifying a distribution summary and outliers. Histograms are better for seeing the frequency distribution within specific intervals. ::: {#403d3fd9 .cell execution_count=47} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.boxplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', y='island', hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-48-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#d866d84f .cell execution_count=48} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.boxplot( data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', y='island', hue='sex', fliersize=8, # fliersize: size of outlier points (default: 5) ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-49-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#795a829f .cell execution_count=49} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.boxplot( data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', y='island', hue='sex', fliersize=8, whis=2, # whisker: extend to Q1/Q3 +/- 2*IQR (default: 1.5); larger values reduce outlier points ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-50-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.boxplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.boxplot.html)** (`fliersize` and `whis` parameters) ## Violin Plot A violin plot combines features of a box plot, such as medians and quantiles, with a density curve that shows the smoothed distribution. When the dataset is small, the smoothed curve may be misleading, so a histogram or box plot may be preferable. ::: {#ebac3988 .cell execution_count=50} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.violinplot(data=df, y='island', x='flipper_length_mm', hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-51-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} ::: ::: ::: {#2b77882d .cell execution_count=51} ``` {.python .cell-code} # split=True: combine the two hue groups in the same category into one violin for easier distribution comparison sns.violinplot( data=df, y='island', x='flipper_length_mm', hue='sex', split=True, # Combine two hue groups into one violin for easier comparison ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-52-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} ::: ::: **Reference: [`sns.violinplot()` documentation](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.violinplot.html)** (`split` parameter) ## Strip Plot and Swarm Plot **Strip plots** draw every data point, with each dot representing one observation. Points are randomly jittered along the categorical axis to reduce overlap. **Swarm plots** automatically arrange overlapping data points and are easier to read. Note that both plots show a univariate **distribution**, meaning how densely one variable appears across its range. This is different from a scatter plot, which shows the **relationship** between two variables. | Comparison | Strip Plot | Swarm Plot | |-------------------|----------------------------|-------------------------| | Basic idea | Randomly jitter data points along the categorical axis to avoid overlap | Precisely arrange points with an algorithm to avoid overlap and show the distribution | | Point placement | Random jitter; overlap may still occur | Non-random; automatically adjusted by density to avoid overlap | | Readability | Clear for small datasets; can overlap heavily with large datasets | Clearer for showing distribution shape in small to medium datasets | | Computational cost | Lower and faster to draw | Higher and slower for large datasets | | Suitable uses | Quick visualization, small datasets, situations where exact distribution shape is less important | Showing distribution details for medium-sized datasets | | Distribution detail | Moderate; true density can be hard to see | Stronger; data density is easier to read visually | | Parameter control | Jitter can be controlled with `jitter` | No jitter needed; the algorithm adjusts placement automatically | | Example function | `sns.stripplot()` | `sns.swarmplot()` | ::: {#36996a77 .cell execution_count=52} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.stripplot(data=df, x='flipper_length_mm', y='island', hue='sex') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/cell-53-output-1.png){width=653 height=440} :::
